body: A few things that would embarrass us if we didn't catch them. First, the big physical picture: this is a one-group pre/post design with no control condition. SART and Ospan are practice-sensitive tasks — people get better the second time just from having seen them. So even a 'significant improvement' can't be attributed to the decluttering; the wiggle in the arrow could be pure test-retest learning. The spec's success criteria (SC-001 through SC-004) read as if a pre-post change answers the causal question, but the validation section called this 'a causal inquiry about an intervention's effect' — the design shown cannot deliver that. Second, there's an internal contradiction: US-3 scenario 2 says the system should 'prioritize bootstrapped confidence intervals... over a binary normality test switch,' but FR-006 makes the Wilcoxon fallback 'triggered only if Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.05' — i.e., exactly the binary normality-test switch the scenario says to avoid. Third, the attrition math is unanchored: 'at least 34 participants... minimum required for the planned power' — but no total N is stated anywhere and the power analysis is explicitly deferred, so 34 is a number with no derivation behind it. Fourth, PANAS is two scores (positive and negative affect) while FR-008 corrects for 'four outcome variables' — that's five comparisons, and the multiple-comparison family is miscounted. Finally, self-reported social media minutes (FR-010, US-2) is the intervention's dosage measure with no objective check unless a subset happens to provide screen-time data (FR-011) — the compliance data and the outcome data both being self-report weakens the independence the validation section claimed.

A small worked example primes my worry: suppose participants improve on SART from baseline to post-test. In a single-arm pre-post design, that improvement could come from the decluttering — or from practice effects on the cognitive tasks, regression to the mean, or demand characteristics (participants know they're supposed to get calmer). The validation section passed a circularity check, but the design itself has no control condition, and nowhere does the spec acknowledge this. What You See Is All There Is: the spec shows change scores and asks us to read them as intervention effects, and System 1 is happy to comply. A waitlist control arm, or at minimum an explicit limitation, would let System 2 check that leap. Second, the attrition assumption states a minimum analyzable sample of 34 'which is the minimum required for the planned power,' while the same document concedes 'a formal power analysis was not conducted' — the number 34 is asserted, not established. Third, FR-006 is internally inconsistent: bootstrapped CIs are declared primary precisely because Shapiro-Wilk is low-power, yet the Wilcoxon fallback is 'triggered only if Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.05' — the low-power test is made the gatekeeper for a method whose purpose was to avoid it. Fourth, FR-010 flags entries 'identical to 0 for all 7 days' as data quality issues, while the edge case explicitly says to include such participants 'to avoid selection bias'; the flag-then-include path should be reconciled. Finally, SC-004 asks for 'a statistically significant improvement' in PANAS positive/negative affect without defining the direction for negative affect — a reduction, presumably, but the spec should say so.
